In their series Photo Spotlight, Holden Luntz Gallery presents the photographs of Jerry Schatzberg. They introduce him as follows.

JERRY SCHATZBERG AND THE LIFE AROUND PERFORMANCE

Jerry Schatzberg belongs to a rare group of photographers who understood that performance does not begin on stage or end when the curtain falls. In his photographs, the worlds of music, fashion, dance, and celebrity are never reduced to publicity or pose. They appear instead through gesture, rhythm, atmosphere, and presence. His pictures often catch artists before they become fully conscious of the camera, when style and personality still feel spontaneous.

That quality makes Schatzberg especially compelling in the context of music and dance. He photographed many of the defining figures of the 1960s, yet what remains most striking is not simply their fame, but the spontaneity of the images and the contemporary feeling of his photographs. Whether photographing Bob Dylan with a cigarette in his mouth, Jimi Hendrix in a moment of inward concentration, Diana Ross within the charged social world of New York nightlife, or a dancer carried into movement and blur, Schatzberg presents performers as living presences rather than celebrated stars.

A STUDIO AT THE CENTER OF THE CITY

Schatzberg’s rise began in New York, where he began as an assistant to photographer Bill Helburn before opening his own studio on Park Avenue South in the mid-1950s. His photographs soon graced the pages of Vogue, Esquire, Glamour, McCall’s. This period coincided with a moment when American image-making was becoming freer, quicker, and more responsive to the street.

His photographs helped liberate fashion from a predictable statuary pose. His models do not simply display clothes; they walk, turn, laugh, lean, and improvise. That ability to respond and adapt to what was happening in front of him became central to his work. Schatzberg’s studio soon became part of the cultural life of New York in the 1960s. It was a place where musicians, actors, models, dancers, and artists passed through with unusual ease. Even when an image is carefully constructed, it rarely feels overmanaged.

RAPPORT BEFORE THE IMAGE

If there is one word that helps explain Schatzberg’s photographs, it is rapport. Again and again, those who have written about him, or worked with him return to his ability to put people at ease. He liked to spend time talking, joking, and waiting for a mood to emerge before he began photographing. For Schatzberg, that time spent establishing trust, as well as connection, was essential to making the picture.

You can feel this clearly in his portraits of musicians. Bob Dylan, whom Schatzberg photographed repeatedly in the mid-1960s, appears unmistakably himself, yet also unguarded. In Bob Dylan, Smoke, New York, the gesture is simple: one hand partially obscures the face, a cigarette hangs from the mouth, and Dylan’s hair seems to take on a life of its own.

The photograph feels intimate rather than posed. Dylan appears less as a public symbol than as someone caught thinking, pausing, and briefly retreating into himself. Schatzberg understood that personality often reveals itself most clearly through small, unplanned gestures.

That sensitivity extends across his music portraits more broadly. He did not need the concert stage to communicate musical presence. He could find it in posture, wit, fatigue, ease, and stillness. Even at rest, the performer remains fully present.

NIGHTLIFE, MUSIC, AND THE SOCIAL THEATER OF THE 1960s

Schatzberg’s involvement in the music world was not confined to studio sittings. He was also a co-owner of Ondine and, later, Salvation, two New York clubs that became important gathering places within the decade’s nightlife and music scene. The Doors, Buffalo Springfield, Jimi Hendrix, Bob Dylan, the Rolling Stones, Diana Ross, and many others moved through those rooms.

This gives us insight into the social intelligence of Schatzberg’s photographs. He was not chasing or observing celebrity from a distance. He saw musicians where they relaxed, performed informally, danced, flirted, watched one another, and became part of the larger theater of the city.

His pictures from this world carry that familiarity. They do not strain for access because access is already there. What interests him is the energy of the room and the people within it. His subjects are stylish, certainly, but they are also alert, amused, absorbed, unguarded, and often playful.

Schatzberg recognized that performance spills beyond the official frame into clubs, friendships, late nights, and improvised encounters. The culture of music was not only sound. It was posture, timing, social rhythm, and a way of moving through the world.

WHEN THE PHOTOGRAPH LEARNS TO MOVE

What makes Schatzberg such a natural fit for an exhibition centered on music and dance is the importance of movement throughout his work. Sometimes that movement is literal, as in his photographs of dancers and performers. At other times, it appears through angle, blur, or the flow of an action.

In Geoffrey Holder on Stage, the performer seems to dissolve into motion. The body is not crisply fixed but carried into blur, as though Schatzberg has allowed the camera to follow the logic of dance rather than interrupt it. What remains is a sensation of sweep, fabric, and momentum, with the performer passing through the light too quickly for the camera to hold him completely.

That same interest animates Window Washer Ballet, New York, an unexpected symphony of moments. A worker suspended on a ladder becomes a dancer poised in precarious balance against the rigid geometry of the city. A passing car cuts across the foreground, adding another layer of motion and rhythm. The title is playful, but the transformation is real. Schatzberg sees choreography where others might simply see labor. Movement was not limited to his photographs of performers. It shaped the way he saw the city and the people around him.

THE PERFORMER AS PERSON

In consideration of the style, sophistication, and historical importance of Schatzberg’s archive, what endures most is his refusal to let fame flatten a subject into cliché. He photographed stars, but he was never overawed by stardom. He understood that charisma is most powerful when it remains close to the human scale, revealing itself through expression, timing, and personal connection. That is why his work still feels so fresh. He gives us photographs of the great figures of his era, often shifting his focus from the public image to the private self. Music becomes mood, dance becomes gesture, and performance becomes part of everyday life.

Schatzberg’s photographs remind us that the most lasting images of performers are not always the most theatrical. Often, they are the ones in which the subject appears most alive, most fleeting, and most fully present.

Image 79: Our Week Favorite: Marie Mons embarks on a kind of quest for identity in this photographic series, in which she once again explores the theme of the self-portrait. Throughout, she consistently questions appearances: those of her body, those of her own gaze, and those of our own… A reciprocal exchange of questions between the subject, the artist and the viewer, oscillating between certainties (what Marie knows about herself) and discoveries (what the final image might reveal by capturing what eludes us). Marie Mons, ‘Self-Portraits’, published in the journals of the Maison François Méchain @mariemons @lamaisonfrancoismechain Photo: © Marie Mons - Courtesy of the artist — — — — — Notre sélection de la semaine : Marie Mons poursuit une forme de quête d’identité dans cette série photographique où elle creuse à nouveau la question de l’autoportrait. Avec constance, elle y interroge les apparences : celles de son corps, celles de son propre regard, celles du nôtre… Réciprocité des questions entre le modèle, l’artiste et le spectateur, va et vient entre certitudes (ce que Marie sait d’elle-même) et découvertes (ce que l’image finale pourrait révèler en captant ce qui échappe). Image 81: Exhibition: Earlie Hudnall has been photographing Houston’s Third and Fourth Wards since the 1970s. These neighbourhoods have a fascinating African-American history; the Fourth Ward was founded by former freed slaves. Earlie has captured iconic images of Houston’s residents and has enjoyed a long and successful career, with his photographs featured in museum collections across the country. On view in the exhibition ‘From Sea To Shining Sea’ at the PDNB Gallery. @pdnbgallery Photo: Earlie Hudnall, Jr., Jumping Rope, 1997, Courtesy of PDNB Gallery, Denton, TX — — — — — Exposition : Earlie Hudnall photographie les Third et Fourth Wards de Houston depuis les années 1970. Ces quartiers possèdent une histoire afro-américaine passionnante ; le Fourth Ward a été fondé par d’anciens esclaves affranchis. Earlie a saisi des images emblématiques des habitants de Houston et a connu une carrière longue et fructueuse, ses photographies figurant dans des collections de musées à travers tout le pays. Image 83: Biennale: In a landscape where major photography events are often concentrated in large cities, the Xavier Miserachs Photography Biennale champions a different vision of a festival: an event on a human scale that fosters a dialogue between local memory and contemporary issues. And among the Biennale’s many highlights is ‘Travailleurs de la mer’ by Carles Palacio, which focuses on the fishermen of the Costa Brava and the vulnerabilities of a profession under threat. @carlespalacio @biennalxmiserachs Photo: Serie Trabajadores del Mar, Costa Brava, 2018-2022 - Carles Palacio — — — — — Biennale : Dans un paysage où les grands rendez-vous de l’image restent souvent concentrés dans les grandes villes, la Biennale de photographie Xavier Miserachs défend une autre idée du festival ; une manifestation à taille humaine capable de faire dialoguer mémoire locale et enjeux actuels. Et parmi les nombreux points forts de la Biennale, « Travailleurs de la mer » de Carles Palacio, consacré aux pêcheurs de la Costa Brava et aux fragilités d’un métier menacé.

Image 85: Exhibition: 'My practice focuses on identity, emotional experience and the psychological spaces young people navigate, using image‑making to express what is often felt but not easily spoken. I work experimentally with processes such as projection, cyanotype, fabric and layered photographic techniques, creating intimate and reflective pieces grounded in lived experience.' — Sianna Campbell at Travel Through Art Studio. sianacampbell @travelthroughartstudio Photo: © Sianna Campbell — — — — Exposition : « Ma pratique s'articule autour de l'identité, de l'expérience émotionnelle et des espaces psychologiques dans lesquels évoluent les jeunes. Je recourt à la création d'images pour exprimer ce qui est souvent ressenti mais difficilement formulé. Je travaille de manière expérimentale avec des procédés tels que la projection, le cyanotype, le tissu et les techniques photographiques en superposition, afin de créer des œuvres intimes et propices à la réflexion, ancrées dans l'expérience vécue. » — Sianna Campbell, au Travel Through Art Studio. #siennacampbell #traveltroughartstudio

The Hulett Collection presents Alain Laboile : At The End Of The World, highlights from La Famille. Michael Hulett introduces it as follows.

Alain Laboile (b. 1968, Bordeaux) never trained as a photographer. He picked up a camera in 2004 to document his sculpture work and fell into it through a fascination with entomology and macrophotography. In 2007, at 39, he turned the lens on his own growing family, living an unconventional, barefoot life on a rural property outside Bordeaux. The resulting body of work, La Famille, became an international phenomenon: featured by the New York Times in 2012, published as the monograph À la Fin du Monde (Kehrer Verlag, 2015), and now held in the permanent collection of the Musée français de la photographie. Self-taught and still shooting his six children as they grow, Laboile captures childhood as a suspended, timeless world, equal parts tenderness, wildness, and myth.

I first learned of Alain’s work through a UK client who had just purchased several of his prints. I reached out to him, unprompted, and asked if we could work together. That was nearly five years ago. The work is just as powerful today as it was the first time I experienced it.

Michael Hulett

The Hulett Collection1311 E 15th St,

Tulsa, OK 74120.

On view for eleven days on the walls of the Ramallah Contemporary Arts Festival 2026, Mélissa Waucquier’s Fair Mur is a public photographic installation comprising portraits, rehearsal scenes and candid moments.

Pasted up as the project progresses to form an evolving collective mural accessible to the public at all times, the photographs by the French photographer and artistic director – founder of MW Creation (Nice) – seek to document a performing arts festival in Palestine in 2026, and in doing so, choose to prioritise beauty, movement, joy, and the persistence of creativity as photographic subject matter, rather than images of war and devastation.

Mélissa Waucquier sent us this text:

‘What I remember first is the gentleness. Cardamom coffee first thing in the morning. The warm air. The terraces full of people late into the night.

Men bent over a game of dominoes. Women smoking shisha with friends.

I walk.

Filled with a strange joy. A tear welling up in the corner of my eye that returns without warning.

Very quickly, I no longer know what I came here to find. Every encounter shifts the images I had brought with me.

I am still searching for the words. The ones that tell a story without oversimplifying.

The ones that bear witness without claiming to explain.

I came to Ramallah to create a photographic installation for the Ramallah Contemporary Art Festival.

Photography has always been my way of reaching out to others. It gives me the courage to ask a question I wouldn’t otherwise ask.

May I take your photograph?

For me, that question is already a way of sharing the image.

I don’t want it to belong entirely to me.

Every photograph is, first and foremost, an encounter.

Every day, on my way up to Beit Al Saa, I pass an old, worn armchair sitting in an alleyway.

I hope that one morning someone will sit down in it.

Hekmet is there.

May I take your photograph?

We see each other every day. We don’t speak the same language. We share sunflower seeds, smiles, a few gestures. One day, she hands me a photograph – it’s her during the first Intifada, facing the Israeli army. A fighter.

By agreeing to this portrait, she is not just entrusting me with her face.

She is also entrusting me with a fragment of her story.

On the opening day, she walks through the doors of the exhibition.

That is perhaps what I love most about photography: everything an image makes possible even before it exists.

In the evening, I capture the performances. I discover a culture that moves me deeply, even in works I do not fully understand. I have seen entire auditoriums laugh and cry in the same breath.

Artists dancing, loving, creating, whilst war permeates the conversations, the stories, the absences, and sometimes the bodies themselves.

Nothing denies the violence. Nothing surrenders life to it. Joy and sorrow do not follow one another.

They coexist.

On the final evening, Saleh Bakri pays tribute to his father, Mohammad Bakri.

He says: ‘I am stronger than Israel. Stronger through my tenderness. Through my love for my family. Through my humanity. Through my creativity.’ I believe it was at that moment that something clicked within me.

I take away a certainty. We can carry memory without giving up joy. Weep and laugh on the same day. Drink coffee for hours on end.

To dance whilst knowing to hold both

I leave with more questions than answers. And with a responsibility. To look after the stories entrusted to me.

These images do not tell the story of Palestine.

They tell the story of the Palestine I encountered.”

TBW Books announces the publication of Bell Pond, a new monograph by artist Stephen DiRado.

Bell Pond documents the summer of 1983 at a public swimming pond in Worcester, Massachusetts, where DiRado spent months photographing the community that gathered there. Arriving one afternoon on a whim during an early heat wave, he introduced himself to anyone willing to pay attention—and kept coming back. Working with a large-format camera on a tripod, he distributed prints, and slowly became part of the community’s fabric, earning the trust of those who might otherwise have had little reason to give it. That trust was hard won and freely returned—by summer’s end, DiRado had become a fixture, his daily arrival an event in itself.

The resulting portraits are unparalleled in their intimacy—and together they build a vivid portrait of the place and its inhabitants. DiRado moved between families, friends, couples, and individuals—capturing the textures of a working-class community that claimed Bell Pond as its own. The work is a timestamp of a world before the internet and the endless digital reproduction of likenesses. Through DiRado’s lens, these lives are given weight and permanence—crystallized on film in a way the world around them rarely afforded. Whole stories exist within each frame, and the mystery of what we’ll never fully know pushes to the foreground. DiRado stayed close to many of his subjects long after that summer ended, invested in them as people, not just as photographs.

What runs through every image is DiRado’s deep humanism. These are people society too often passes over, and here they are seen clearly, without sentimentality, and without looking away.

Sure enough, the tireless Hans Silvester is launching a new exhibition just a few kilometers from the previous one. In terms of setting, this second show has nothing to envy to the first the same type of thirteenth-century castle. It is within the walls of the medieval fortress of Gréoux that a cohesive selection of Hans’s Camargue works is on display.

This new exhibition has been organized and coordinated by the Friends of Jean Giono, in this commemorative year. These admirers of the great Provençal writer obtained permission from Hans Silvester, from Jean Giono’s family, and from his publisher, to produce a modernized reprint of a thousand copies of “Camargue.” This book was born, originally, of the unlikely collaboration between the young, highly determined photographer and the master of Provençal literature a reprint whose significance I gave you to when it went to press back in May.

It is in close collaboration with the town of Gréoux-les-Bains that the Friends of Jean Giono were able to take over the château’s entrance and its superb guardroom. The site’s manager and the association’s tireless secretary provided the kind of technical support any creator would dream of. Hans seized on this potential, selecting from his vast photographic archives the Camargue images that are in perfect harmony with Jean Giono’s literary spirit. The result is stunning an exhibition of the kind we love and that has become increasingly rare, both in venues built for it and amid the multitude of large-scale events, all those potential cultural platforms that have become overused and often distorted.

Everything is perfectly coherent, from the magical setting to the subtle prints of the works, by way of a clear-sighted scenography and good hanging. The majesty and serenity of the setting create an inevitable connection (with the necessary physical distance) between the viewers and the photographs.

All these images were chosen by their author with the greatest qualitative care, in the spirit of a Jean Giono who liked to efface himself within his own stories. His lines, words upon words, as lyrical as they are poetic about the Camargue countryside, carry his spirit forward. It is this carefree poetry that dominates every image hung on the walls.

Whether you’re completely passionate about photography or not don’t hesitate to make your way to the Château de Gréoux-les-Bains. A mental escape and the allure of dreams are guaranteed. It’s a truly refreshing break from your daily race against time.

Sincere thanks to the Cultural Department of the City of Gréoux and to the volunteer teams of the Friends of Jean Giono for putting this exhibition together. Kudos to Hans Silvester, who consistently delivers high-quality photographs and manages to keep up with the pace required to handle all the very different exhibitions that call on his services.

Thierry Maindrault

EXHIBITION

Jean Giono et la PhotoChâteau de Gréoux

07 place de l’Hôtel de ville

04800 GREOUX LES BAINS

phone +33 4 92 78 01 08

opening hours 2 p.m. to 6 p.m.

Free admission.

Image 79: Our Week Favorite: Marie Mons embarks on a kind of quest for identity in this photographic series, in which she once again explores the theme of the self-portrait. Throughout, she consistently questions appearances: those of her body, those of her own gaze, and those of our own… A reciprocal exchange of questions between the subject, the artist and the viewer, oscillating between certainties (what Marie knows about herself) and discoveries (what the final image might reveal by capturing what eludes us). Marie Mons, ‘Self-Portraits’, published in the journals of the Maison François Méchain @mariemons @lamaisonfrancoismechain Photo: © Marie Mons - Courtesy of the artist — — — — — Notre sélection de la semaine : Marie Mons poursuit une forme de quête d’identité dans cette série photographique où elle creuse à nouveau la question de l’autoportrait. Avec constance, elle y interroge les apparences : celles de son corps, celles de son propre regard, celles du nôtre… Réciprocité des questions entre le modèle, l’artiste et le spectateur, va et vient entre certitudes (ce que Marie sait d’elle-même) et découvertes (ce que l’image finale pourrait révèler en captant ce qui échappe). https://loeildelaphotographie.com/en/arc.content:
Archives – August 7, 2020

It is a place where time fades away. A place where the physical contours of matter dissolve.

Here photography recovers the delicacy of the nineteenth-century pictorialists. In this body of work Stéphane Mahé opens a window onto an intangible elsewhere and invites us to step to one side, in search of a second reality. Somewhere at the edge of the world.

Place and time matter little… here the one who looks interprets, invents, tells their own story, their own stories.

Somewhere is a sequence of images that come together like a feverish breath, within which each photograph is nonetheless autonomous and offers the eye the possibility of a beginning.

Somewhere is, of course, somewhere; somewhere between yesterday and tomorrow, somewhere between the street corner and the far end of the field; a place so familiar and yet, by a single detail, so different that you want to come and quietly lose yourself in it.

Stéphane Mahé: Somewhere

August 1 – September 12, 2020

La chambre claire Galerie

3 rue Voltaire

Douarnenez (29100)

The Shadow of the Duende

In this series of Flamenco portraits, light and shadow clash to reveal the truth of the body: the intensity of a gaze, the pinpoint precision of a gesture, the dramatic tension of the moment. My goal is to help you feel the inner power and raw poetry of these dancers, where the soul lays itself bare.

The deliberate choice of high-contrast black and white has allowed me to strip the image down to its essence, conveying raw emotion. Each image is a moment suspended in time, a fleeting instant captured between two clicks of the heels, in which I seek to capture the inner essence of the performers, beyond mere technique. To reveal that intimate moment,that state of grace,when the artist is overcome by that mysterious, visceral, yet ever-vibrant force known as the duende.

https://loeildelaphotographie.com/en/son.content:
Common Matter

“COMMON MATTER”, a photographic project by Sonia Fattori, explores the ancestral bond between humans and the natural environment. Using a combination of human portraits and natural landscapes, the project proposes a comparison between human and natural anatomy, highlighting what unites them.

The photographic focus is on the very essence of matter and surface: from skin marked by the sun to the grooves of time on faces and stone; from the lines of bodies to the geometry of the landscape; from the colors of fabrics to the shades of layered rocks, suggesting that individuals carry within themselves, in a tangible and visible way, the territory they inhabit.

The aim of the work is to highlight the deep connection between humans and nature, emphasizing how these two entities coexist and mutually influence each other, drawing attention to the need to rethink a relationship that risks becoming increasingly unnatural and disrespectful. Humans do not merely inhabit the land; they are part of it and, as such, must relate to it—at the cost of their own survival.

For the landscape images, the territory of the Province of Salta (Argentina) was chosen, where indigenous populations are working to resist the dominant predatory culture and to defend their identity, founded on a relationship with the land that is not economic but spiritual, communal, and vital, characterized by reciprocity and a deep respect for natural cycles.

The human faces and figures, instead, come from India (Rajasthan), the cradle of one of the richest, most ancient, and enduring cultures in human history, whose history seems to be imprinted on these faces, making them living testimony.

The harmony and commonality perceived in the juxtaposition of geographically distant places and people dissolve physical boundaries and suggest a path toward recognizing a single identity and a shared destiny of humanity, closely tied to the relationship it establishes and maintains with the environment. The resemblance between human geography and the landscape, as well as the effects of time and weathering on both humans and nature, evokes the idea of a “common matter,” and also of a shared matrix, so that the destiny of one becomes the destiny of the other, and nothing humans do to the environment fails to have repercussions on themselves as well.

The project also encourages us to lift our gaze from these images—of a simple, sometimes harsh, yet spontaneous and harmonious belonging—and turn it toward our own places, the environments of everyday life across almost all latitudes, to seek confirmation of the inseparable bond that human beings establish with them and the destiny they thereby write.

As land decreases and concrete increases, colors become less varied, rhythms less natural, food more processed and packaged… Across many fronts we witness a separation, a distancing, a loss of balance and well-being, but perhaps we still have the opportunity to reaffirm our common essence.

A project by Sonia Fattori, texts by Marta Daneluzzi

Syzygie//Eadem

History. Collisions. Here, moments of life on the islands of the Gironde Estuary are interwoven. I weave my photographs of these islands with anonymous or family photographs to create an unverifiable yet probable reality, imagined and enviable. The game is to reformulate a legend by provoking an identity based on supposition and invention, according to the actual story. Some anonymous photographs truly show the estuary, others, without any identifying information, raise doubts, most not at all. The aim is to play on memory and plausibility: “it looks like the estuary,” “these people could be islanders,” “it looks like Aunt Angèle.” The desire is to explore the imagination. The juxtaposition with photographs of my family signifies my attachment to these islands, illustrates the echo with my own story. Thus creating an anachronistic continuity. An identification, an empathy, a transfer, a tribute. Weaving paths, disrupting legends and photographic irresolutions. Continuing to knit the threads of memory and time.

‘Syzygy’ is the alignment or opposition of the moon, sun, and Earth. It refers to the periods of the new or full moon that give rise to the tides. It is union, correspondence, alignment, flow, connection, separation, harmony, temporality.

‘Eadem’ means “by the same path” in Latin.

Anonymous analog photograph, family portrait, digital photograph, (2015-2026/)

Αμμόχωστος – Το Άλγος του Νόστου | Ammochostos – The Algos of Hostos

No one enters Varosha innocently. To look is already to become witness to a violation that continues.

This is not an artist statement. This is a visual deposition of an ongoing war crime.

Varosha, Famagusta, Cyprus, October 2020.

For the enclosed city of Ammochostos (Famagusta), time seems to have stood still since 1974, frozen in a surreal cinematic set. Today it is enveloped in an altogether different aura, both as a place and a landscape.

In 1974, under the pretext of protecting the Turkish Cypriots, Turkey invaded the island following a short-lived coup instigated and orchestrated by the Greek Junta. Since then, Turkey unlawfully occupies one-third of the Republic of Cyprus, trampling upon any notion of international legality.

Based on United Nations Security Council resolutions 550 (1984) and 789 (1992), the city of Famagusta should have been placed under the control of the United Nations. However, in blatant violation of these resolutions, Turkey continues to occupy the entire city. Its most vibrant part, Varosha, an area of 6.2 square kilometers, was fenced off and placed under military control, to be used as a bargaining chip in the talks for a Cyprus settlement.

In a provocative illegality, the occupation regime in October 2020 opened part of the fenced city of Ammochostos, converting the deserted city usurped from its lawful Greek inhabitants into a grotesque theme park under the misleading guise of a tourist destination.

The new reality imposed upon the city functions as a constant reminder and exploitation of pain. Unknowingly and unwillingly, each of us becomes a witness to an ongoing, relentless violation in a frozen conflict.

Nocturne

Nocturne is a portrait series built around the tension between concealment and exposure. Through darkness, close framing, restrained gestures, and shifts between black fabric and bare skin, the work explores how presence changes when a person is partially hidden and partially revealed.

The series moves between distance and intimacy. Hair, shadow, posture, and gaze become visual barriers, but also points of contact. Rather than constructing a fixed character, Nocturne focuses on a state: quiet, vulnerable, controlled, and slightly unsettling.

The project was recently published in MALVIE Magazine, Body Positivity Edition, June 2026.

https://loeildelaphotographie.com/en/flo.content:
The Invisible Within Reach

Every day we move through cities inhabited by thousands of lives. Faces, gestures, glances—individual existences crossing paths without ever truly meeting.

Through familiarity, we stop looking. We recognize silhouettes before remembering that they are people.

This series was born from that quiet observation.

Throughout my walks, I sought those fleeting moments when a presence seems to fade away: a traveler lost in an empty station, a figure dissolving into light, a homeless person becoming almost invisible within the urban landscape, a woman absorbed by the horizon, a passerby reduced to nothing more than a reflection.

None of these photographs seeks to explain or accuse.

They simply offer a moment of stillness.

Black and white strips reality of distraction, revealing what remains essential: light, space, silence, and the fragile place of human beings in a world that never stops accelerating.

These photographs speak less about the people we see than about the way we choose to see them.

For the invisible is not always the one who hides.

Sometimes, it is simply the one our gaze quietly allows to disappear.

https://loeildelaphotographie.com/en/the.content:
Klavdij Sluban: The Image Against Evidence

There are photographers who show us the world. Klavdij Sluban belongs to that much rarer breed who question it. For him, photography does not document; it clarifies. It seeks neither proof nor spectacle, nor even the decisive moment. It moves against the tide of time, at a deliberately unhurried pace, until reality ceases to be an obvious fact and becomes a question. Born in Slovenia and arriving in France as a teenager, Sluban has spent more than three decades developing a body of work that stubbornly resists categorisation. Neither documentary nor conceptual, nor truly belonging to the realm of visual art, his photography is above all a form of writing. Each image is conceived as a fragment, a breath, a punctuation mark within a larger body of work in which correspondences matter more than the subjects themselves. Borders, peripheral territories, juvenile prisons, the Balkans, the Trans-Siberian Railway, the Kerguelen Islands and buried memories are less themes than places from which to contemplate absence, transmission and the fragility of the gaze. The black and white he employs with an almost ascetic rigour becomes a language rather than an aesthetic. A recipient of the Prix Niépce and an educator who has worked with incarcerated teenagers for more than thirty years, Sluban advocates a form of photography that resists the immediate consumption of images. At a time when images proliferate to the point of exhausting their own meaning, he insists on the time required for maturation, memory and silence. He says, moreover, that he never “takes” photographs, but “makes” them. His entire philosophy is contained in that distinction. For a photograph, in his view, is not born at the moment the shutter is released, but in everything that precedes it: a prolonged absorption of the world, until an image finally agrees to exist.

This reflection finds a particularly resonant echo today in Solitudes insulaires, on view at the Abbaye de La Celle until November 1st 2026, in partnership with the Rencontres de la photographie d’Arles. More than an exhibition, the project unfolds as an inward journey in which two photographic bodies of work the Kerguelen Islands and Japan converge around a shared experience of insularity.On one side, the austere landscapes of “the Island of Desolation”, where human beings appear only in proportion to their own fragility against the mineral immensity of the landscape; on the other, a Japan in which the island becomes a state of consciousness, an inhabited, almost spiritual solitude. Within the minimalist spaces of the former Cistercian abbey, whose silence seems to answer that of the images, the photographs cease to be mere representations and become places of contemplation. Faithful to his refusal of staging, Sluban pursues here the same quest: to make photography not the story of a territory, but the sensory experience of being present in the world.

Site Web: www.lemasterklass.comInstagram: @klavdijsluban

CURRENT EXHIBITION“SOLITUDES INSULAIRES” UNTIL 1 NOVEMBER 2026**ABBAYE DE LA CELLE

DEPARTMENTAL CENTRE FOR PHOTOGRAPHIC ART**9 Place des Ormeaux

83170 La Celle, France**

“I Don’t Take Pictures, I Make Photographs”

What first triggered your desire to make photographs?Klavdij Sluban: To preserve the memory of my closed one, knowing I would one day be separated from them.

A photographic memory from your childhood?Klavdij Sluban: I was photographed more often than Tito. I spent my childhood in Yugoslavia, and my adoptive family constantly “paparazzied” me so they could send pictures to my parents in France.

What was the camera of your childhood?Klavdij Sluban: Memory.

And the one you use today?Klavdij Sluban: Memory on film.

Who is the image-maker that has inspired you the most?Klavdij Sluban: The person who smeared their dirty hands all over the cave walls.

Was that person considered a good-for-nothing, fit for nothing else? Or were they the living gods or goddesses of the cave? Even then, there was already the question of the positive hand or the negative hand, depending on the technique employed: placing a pigment-covered hand against the rock, or blowing pigment around it. One can easily imagine prehistoric wars between positive hands and negative hands, foreshadowing future massacres between the tribes of colour and the tribes of black and white, the tribes of grain and the tribes of pixels. It also raises the question of artistic precarity or rather, of the mistreatment of photographers in our contemporary economic system, which supports and institutionalises every field of artistic creation except photography. Were those positive and negative hands the prehistoric etymology of the word photographer already starving? Another etymology, this time in modern Greek, for the word photographer. Forty or sixty thousand years before Nicéphore Niépce… How did those triggering hands survive? What share of the mammoth did they receive?

What image would you have liked to make?Klavdij Sluban:In utero.

Which image has moved you the most?Klavdij Sluban: Brezhnev kissing Honecker on the lips.

And which one has made you angry?Klavdij Sluban: Honecker kissing Brezhnev on the lips.

Which photograph changed the world?Klavdij Sluban: None. We’d know if one had.

And which photograph changed your world?Klavdij Sluban: One of those almost ordinary images we’ve seen countless versions of it: refugees in a forest.This time, a young, gaunt woman stands with three terrified children at her feet in a makeshift camp. Around them sit exhausted soldiers, their rifles lying on the ground. Every anonymous figure embodies the archetypes of fear, hunger, despair and the shadow of death.Except that this time it is my grandmother, with her three daughters, who spent the entire Second World War hiding in the forest.My grandfather, was one of the exhausted soldiers and this is the last photograph ever taken of him he was a partisan commander. He died shortly before the Armistice, weapon in hand.

Which image occupies the most important place in your personal pantheon?Klavdij Sluban: All the photographs that will never be shown, yet will never be deleted. They inhabit the foundations of the house, the invisible base of the work in progress. Invisible photographs, yet profoundly alive unlike those displayed on social media, which are often stillborn. I spend my nights explaining to them why they are essential. They ensure the foundations, the stability, the anchoring of the house. The obvious, load-bearing photographs are often full of themselves. The subtler ones are the connecting photographs the ones that build bridges between chapters. I only fall asleep once I have convinced them, reassured them, even restored their pride before they take their place beneath the house. I am at peace with myself only when every photograph is exactly where it belongs, happy to be there.

What interests you most in an image?Klavdij Sluban: Suggestion.

What details do you look for in a face, a landscape, or an object?Klavdij Sluban:The part that evokes the whole.

Elliott Erwitt once said, “Colour is descriptive. Black and white is interpretive.” Do you agree?Klavdij Sluban: Many people have said many things. Someone else once said: “Perception without rules cannot give rise to representation.”

Can technique sometimes take precedence over emotion in photography?Klavdij Sluban: Can technique sometimes take precedence over emotion in love?

Is beauty in photography, for you, purely aesthetic?Klavdij Sluban: Aesthetics without ethics equals cosmetics.

What can make silence visible in a photograph?Klavdij Sluban: When a photograph is deaf.

Does the uniqueness of a photograph lie in the moment or in the staging? Can a photograph be truer than reality?Klavdij Sluban: Reality is a construct of the mind. Through a subjective perception of reality translated in a subjective way, a photograph may generate the representation of reality or at least of one particular reality.

Can a photograph change the way we perceive an event?Klavdij Sluban: A photograph eternalises the event. The photographed event becomes a photograph. Every photograph disguises the event. A photograph points to the moon. The visually illiterate stare at the moon.

Is photography a testimony or a form of manipulation?Klavdij Sluban: “Testimony” and “manipulation” are not always contradictory. The very first photograph does not depict reality, since its exposure time exceeded twenty-four hours, producing absurd shadows across the façades. Nor does the first photograph featuring a human figure Boulevard du Temple record reality. Because of its roughly fifteen-minute exposure, the bustling crowd vanished, leaving only the shoeshiner and his customer. The only thing this image truly proves is that the shoeshiner was a conscientious worker, meticulous, proud of a job well done.It would be interesting to know how many of those fifteen minutes he actually spent polishing those shoes.From a Marxist perspective, might the only real manipulation be that of the worker almost certainly underpaid by the dominant bourgeois? Doesn’t the symbolic value of the upright, elegant bourgeois towering above the labourer bent over his miserable condition already suggest a subliminal representation of class relations in 1838?

What makes a good photograph?Klavdij Sluban: A “good” or a “bad” photograph is a personal judgement, one that differs from person to person.An inhabited photograph is an invitation. It can welcome as many viewers as its surface allows.

In your opinion, what is the essential quality of a good photographer?Klavdij Sluban: Making photographs that rhyme with one another.

How do you choose your projects?Klavdij Sluban: From the depths of the calm sea of despair.

How would you describe your creative process?Klavdij Sluban: So slow it would irritate Niépce.

Is there an upcoming project that is especially close to your heart?Klavdij Sluban: Between 1942 and 1943, twenty members of my Slovenian family died in the concentration camps of Rab Island in Croatia and Gonars in Italy. Today I photograph, record and film the testimonies of the seventeen survivors who are still alive. For decades, Italy denied the existence of these concentration camps. Silvio Berlusconi, with denial, contempt and disrespect, referred to them merely as vacanze forzate—”forced holidays.” That is why I gave this major body of work, begun in 2023 and still ongoing, that title. It involves long walks retracing the deportees’ routes, from one camp to another, from the camps where they were imprisoned back to their villages, across forests and beyond national borders. Like my series on incarcerated teenagers, which I began thirty years ago, this is a deeply personal body of work, written with an author’s voice and grounded in real events. Beyond my photographic interpretation, archives, testimonies, writings and film form the very heart of this project.

Who would you most like to photograph?Klavdij Sluban: The wind.

By whom would you most like to be photographed?Klavdij Sluban: By one of my invisible photographs.

An indispensable photography book?Klavdij Sluban: An illustrated dictionary.

What is the last photograph you made?Klavdij Sluban: I don’t take pictures. I make photographs.

On social media, are you more Instagram, Facebook or TikTok—and why?Klavdij Sluban: Facebook shut down my account because its algorithm detected too many keywords such as “prison,” “disciplinary camps,” and “Russia.”

Instagram is useful for sharing professional information.

What has changed in photography since the rise of social media?Klavdij Sluban: The inflationary accumulation of photographs on social media has created a thick layer of images that have never been carried within oneself, that have never experienced latency, that have never been given the time to reveal themselves, to open their eyes. Premature images piling up before they have even had the chance to exist.Yet manure is an excellent fertilizer. It nourishes whatever demands time, care, knowledge and experience to grow. It nourishes what we carry within ourselves before its birth and accompany patiently until it reaches maturity. It takes a long time before one acquires the intimate conviction that a photograph is ready to be revealed.

One Instagram account everyone should follow?Klavdij Sluban:Follow the GuideTHE GUIDE — Follow the guide!

A TOURIST — I am the guide.

HIS DOG — I am my master.

A BEAUTIFUL WOMAN — I am the guide. Therefore I am not a woman, since I am a man.

THE TOURIST — I am that beautiful woman.

THE DOG — And so am I, because I am my master.

THE GUIDE — Follow the guide. I am not the guide, because I am the guide.

THE TOURIST — I would very much like to know who this beautiful woman is that I happen to be.

THE DOG — I am not my master, because I am my master, and that bores me.

THE BEAUTIFUL WOMAN — I am the guide. I am the crowd. I am a regime. I am fashion. I am no longer a child… Oh! I’ve had enough! I am no longer anyone. (She disappears.)THE GUIDE — Oh! I’ve had enough! I resign. (He disappears.)THE TOURIST — Oh! I am no longer the guide, no longer a man, no longer a woman. I am nothing anymore. (He disappears.)THE DOG — At last! I am no longer my master; therefore I am my master, and I shall not be visiting the Loire Valley châteaux!

— Jacques Prévert, FatrasTHE PHOTOGRAPHER — I am no longer Instagram. I am nothing. I am everything. And I shall not photograph the Loire Valley châteaux.

What is your view of AI?Klavdij Sluban: My life is AI: Intense Love.

Colour or black and white?Klavdij Sluban: Your mother or your father?

Natural light or artificial light?Klavdij Sluban: The undoing of darkness.

Which city strikes you as the most photogenic?Klavdij Sluban: An invisible city with an unobstructed view.

Which city, country or culture do you dream of discovering?Klavdij Sluban: AI.

A place you never tire of?Klavdij Sluban: Her face.

Hegel’s image about the owl of Minerva (wisdom) only spreading its wings with the coming of dusk can be taken to mean that, after flapping its wings and flying off into an approaching darkness, an insight is left behind that will later come to light. Meaning emerges retrospectively, interpretation only comes into existence after the event, so there is no way of being sure how the present will be understood in the future. No straight line leads from episodes in the past to our present understanding of them; we shape the past as much as we are shaped by it. Beard’s The End of the Game first appeared over sixty years ago but only now does his achievement come into the light.

First appearing in 1965, Beard rewrote parts of it for a second edition in 1977 and the current Taschen publication gives it another shape with additional material from contributors and a conservationist’s interview with the author. The book has evolved over time and what we see now is a complex and not always consistent compilation of photographs and texts that raises unsettling questions.

The 1965 book was written by someone in his mid-twenties who had been to Kenya when the country was on the cusp of independence. He found himself enraptured by the wildlife and perhaps this helps explain an apparent indifference to certain realities of Kenya’s colonial history. A photo of scaffolding for public executions in Mombasa is slipped in amongst vintage hunting shots but is not commented on; more demanding of the author’s attention is Mackinder’s 1899 ascent of Mount Kenya and of his meeting with Karen Blixen. At times, colonialists’ vocabulary and stereotyping informs the writing: describing the building of the Mombasa-Nairobi railway, he writes of ‘coolies’ recruited from India to build it due to the ‘complete disinclination’ of the ‘native population’ to work.

Such infelicities of language aside, Beard is conflicted about ‘the coming of the white man who imposed his steel tracks’ in a land where ‘nature herself had always been sovereign’. His point, after recording the grim record of the human cost of building the railway, is an ecological one: the balance of nature has been disturbed: the land was an Eden and it has been invaded. This is a familiar trope and it is played out in the book’s movement between fond reminiscences of safari experiences and a photographic record of the catastrophic event that saw thousands of elephants starving to death in Tsavo National Park in the 1970s. His wordless depiction of that disaster takes its place alongside the book’s amassed collection of historical photographs showing hunters posing next to the animal they have killed. The cumulative effect is a palimpsest of slaughter, one traced back to the gentlemen hunters of past times, indicative of Beard’s interest in photography as a form of documentation.

Any response to The End of the Game has to be a complicated one. The book is a paradoxical mix of insight and nostalgia, prescient and romantic, and the conclusion Beard draws about human nature gives him little hope: ‘We’re a scourge from which the planet may never recover’, he tells an interviewer. Paul Theroux, in a foreword to the book, gives coruscating expression to what Beard himself came to feel about the continuation of the ‘game’ begun by privileged white men in Africa. Theroux’s list of those who now make use of the continent includes ‘the child buyer, the retailer of dirty drugs or toxic cigarettes, the experimenting economist, the diamond merchant…the eco-tourist, the adventure travellers, the bird watcher …the banker.., the bullshitter and your cousin the Peace Corp volunteer’. His list is as relentless in its indictment as the photographs Beard brings together in his book and — now that the owl of Minerva has flown — his achievement can be assessed in retrospect.

Sean Sheehan

The End Of The Game

Taschen

Peter Beard

Size: 24.5 x 27.2 cm

The work of Marlo Pascual, a prescient and thought-provoking American artist who stretched the boundaries of photography, is on view at the National Museum of Women in the Arts (NMWA).Marlo Pascual: Making Something Out of Something, the first solo museum exhibition of Pascual’s work in 15 years,introduces viewers to an artist who developed a practice of manipulating found images, creating works that blur the line between photography and sculpture. Pascual worked in the tradition of the “Pictures” generation of artists, such as Barbara Kruger and Cindy Sherman, and recognition of her work was just gaining momentum when she died of cancer at the age of 48 in 2020.

Marlo Pascual (1972–2020) created photo-based works that amuse, confuse, and provoke viewers. Pascual primarily used found imagery of anonymous and often glamorous women from vintage or thrifted sources, which she then dramatically remixed or recontextualized with the addition of sculptural elements. Drawn from NMWA’s collection,Marlo Pascual: Making Something Out of Something presents 17 of Pascual’s works made between 2009 and 2014.

“The exhibition not only introduces visitors to the work of this visionary artist but also preserves Pascual’s legacy,” said Virginia Treanor, NMWA Senior Curator. “We are proud to be ongoing champions of her work, which, through the transformations of seemingly familiar images, challenges us to see the world around us in new ways.”

Through her interventions, Pascual exaggerated and highlighted the artifice of the vintage images she chose. Frequently encasing the enlarged images in thick Plexiglas and pairing them with common yet unexpected objects, Pascual gave them a new aesthetic function. By enlarging them well beyond their intended size, Pascual asserted the physicality of the images, giving them volume and form, akin to sculpture.

Pascual spoke of choosing imagery that she felt was “overtly constructed,” such as studio portraits, yearbook photos, and advertisements. The artist noted, “I think about the construction of the image—how it’s a fragment, and not the whole story, not the truth with a capital ‘T.’”

Pascual’s work transforms what is familiar and even nostalgic into something uncanny, prompting deeper contemplation of what is often taken for granted. Heads, hands, arms, and legs appear disconnected from the rest of the body and become compositional elements of the larger whole. Her process, a creative metamorphosis, can be unsettling, as viewers perceive an emotional tension between beauty and destruction.

In a series of eight photographs in the exhibition, a portrait of a young blond woman is repeatedly obscured by objects and shadows—including a hand, a spiderweb, a table, and flowers. Whether intended as humorous or sinister, these incongruous elements call attention to the artist’s manipulation and, by extension, the artifice of the original image.

In another work, Pascual flipped a bust-length portrait of a woman upside down and positioned the head and neck at a ninety-degree angle beside the torso. She then placed a table lamp directly on top of the woman’s face, obscuring it completely. In this way, the portrait of the woman becomes the physical support for this common household item, relegating her to the same inanimate status.

“As many of Pascual’s fragmentary images are of women, it is hard not to view her works as commentary on the objectification of women that such ‘overtly constructed’ imagery sustains,” notes Treanor. “The transformation of the images into large, stationary objects, which often serve as support for domestic objects like lamps or candleholders, seems to bring the absurdity of ‘woman as object’ to its inevitable, irrational conclusion.”

As Pascual explained her approach to found objects, “I’m not destroying them. I like to think I’m giving them a new life.”

About Marlo Pascual

Tennessee-born and Philadelphia-based artist Marlo Pascual obtained her MFA from the Tyler School of Art (Philadelphia) in 2007. Despite having applied to study photography, her approach to the medium shifted when she experimented with pouring paint over a photograph. She had solo exhibitions at the Swiss Institute, New York, in 2009, and the Aspen Art Museum, Colorado, in 2010. Her work was included in What Is a Photograph?, a 2014 survey at New York’s International Center of Photography. Work by Pascual is in the collections of the Whitney Museum of American Art, New York; Museum of Contemporary Art Chicago; Walker Art Center, Minneapolis; and Pérez Art Museum, Miami.

National Museum of Women in the Arts

The National Museum of Women in the Arts (NMWA) is the first museum in the world solely dedicated to championing women through the arts. With its collections, exhibitions, programs, and online content, the museum inspires dynamic exchanges about art and ideas. NMWA advocates for better representation of women and nonbinary artists and serves as a vital center for thought leadership, community engagement and social change. NMWA addresses the gender imbalance in the presentation of art by bringing to light important women artists of the past while promoting great women artists working today. The collection highlights a wide range of works in a variety of mediums by artists including Rosa Bonheur, Louise Bourgeois, Lalla Essaydi, Lavinia Fontana, Frida Kahlo, Hung Liu, Zanele Muholi, Faith Ringgold, Niki de Saint Phalle, and Amy Sherald.

NMWA is located at 1250 New York Avenue, NW, Washington, DC 20005, two blocks north of Metro Center. The museum is open from 10 a.m.–5 p.m. Tuesday through Sunday; closed Mondays and select holidays. Admission is $16 for adults, $13 for D.C. residents, visitors 65 and over, students and educators, active-duty military and veterans, and visitors with a Native/Tribal Affiliation; and free for visitors 21 and under, visitors with disabilities, and SNAP/EBT card holders. Admission is free the first Sunday and second Wednesday of each month. Contact us at 202-783-5000. Stay connected at: nmwa.org, on the museum’s Broad Strokes blog, Facebook or Instagram.

TBW Books announces the publication of Bell Pond, a new monograph by artist Stephen DiRado.

Bell Pond documents the summer of 1983 at a public swimming pond in Worcester, Massachusetts, where DiRado spent months photographing the community that gathered there. Arriving one afternoon on a whim during an early heat wave, he introduced himself to anyone willing to pay attention—and kept coming back. Working with a large-format camera on a tripod, he distributed prints, and slowly became part of the community’s fabric, earning the trust of those who might otherwise have had little reason to give it. That trust was hard won and freely returned—by summer’s end, DiRado had become a fixture, his daily arrival an event in itself.

The resulting portraits are unparalleled in their intimacy—and together they build a vivid portrait of the place and its inhabitants. DiRado moved between families, friends, couples, and individuals—capturing the textures of a working-class community that claimed Bell Pond as its own. The work is a timestamp of a world before the internet and the endless digital reproduction of likenesses. Through DiRado’s lens, these lives are given weight and permanence—crystallized on film in a way the world around them rarely afforded. Whole stories exist within each frame, and the mystery of what we’ll never fully know pushes to the foreground. DiRado stayed close to many of his subjects long after that summer ended, invested in them as people, not just as photographs.

What runs through every image is DiRado’s deep humanism. These are people society too often passes over, and here they are seen clearly, without sentimentality, and without looking away.

https://loeildelaphotographie.com/en/arc.content:
Archives – August 10, 2022

Oliviero Toscani, one of the most well-known photographers on an international level, was capable of breaking the mould and undermining certainties that appeared permanent in the last decades of the twentieth century. On the occasion of his 80th birthday, the Municipality of Milan celebrates the event at Palazzo Reale, hosting the exhibition Oliviero Toscani. Professione fotografo, that collects his works from the early 1960s to the present day.

The exhibition features 800 photographs by Toscani, including some of his iconic works as well as lesser-known works, thus telling about his career as a man with an ingenious and provocative perspective, who over decades has been influencing the habits of several generations.

His images can be recognized, even though they do not report any logo or signature, as he always used the advertising medium without showing the product, thus making his photography applicable to any brand’s communication. As a photographer and an artist, he knows how to communicate through the graphic sign: he feels the advertising channel as a means and never an end. Even the mass media (newspapers, magazines, and street posters) are part of his language.

Among the photos on stage, there are the iconic Jesus Jeans “Chi mi ama mi segua” poster, Bacio tra prete e suora (1992), Tre Cuori White/Black/Yellow from 1996, No-Anorexia (2007), fashion images (from Donna Jordan to Claudia Schiffer and Monica Bellucci), and those from the period of his training at Zurich’s Kunstgewerbeschule. There are also portraits of personalities like Mick Jagger, Lou Reed, Carmelo Bene, Federico Fellini, and leading figures in culture from the 1970s on. The exhibition is also an opportunity to look at a selection of the Human Race project, with which Oliviero Toscani visited hundreds of places around the world shooting anyone who so wished: the result is the largest existing photographic archive on humankind’s morphological and social differences, with more than 10.000 portraits.

The exhibition is staged without sections or chronological order, like a flow of images showing Toscani’s commitment to the world of fashion, reporting, advertising, culture, portraits, and experimentation, along with original copies of Colors Magazine, founded and led by Toscani, and some videos he directed.

With his photos, Toscani prompted the world to address issues such as racism, death penalty, AIDS, and war, anorexia. He started creating his disruptive images just during the rebellious years, the ones of the Beatles and the Rolling Stones, of Mary Quant’s miniskirts and the students’ protests. During the 70s, he moved to New York, where he frequented Andy Warhol’s Factory as well as the Club 54 and photographed the protagonists of the music and art scenes: Mick Jagger, Joe Cocker, Lou Reed, among others.

Many iconic corporate images and advertising campaigns for Esprit, Chanel, Robe di Kappa, Fiorucci, Prenatal, Jesus, Inter, Toyota, the Italian Ministries of Labour and Health, Artemide, Woolworth, just to quote some, were created by Toscani. A quite compelling case is the one concerning the years between 1982 and 2000.

In 1982 Toscani started signing the campaigns for Benetton, creating a series of iconic photographs. He also created the image, identity and communication strategy of United Colors of Benetton which soon became one of the world’s most well-known brands. In doing so, Toscani used advertising to address serious and urgent matters.

As a fashion photographer, he has worked and still works with magazines like Elle, GQ, Vogue, Harper’s Bazaar, Stern, Esquire, Liberation, and many others. He was also one of the founders of the Mendrisio Academy of Architecture and has taught visual communication in various universities.

The exhibition at the Palazzo Reale venue is promoted by Comune di Milano-Cultura, produced and organized by Palazzo Reale and Arthemisia, and curated by Nicolas Ballario.

Another opportunity to see works by Toscani is the exhibition Oliviero Toscani. 80 anni da situazionista, that’s on at Palazzo Albergati in Bologna. It’s presented by Arthemisia, with over one hundred shots.

The Hulett Collection presents a newly available selection of images from Noell Oszvald‘s ongoing self-portrait series. While some have been published for a number of years, there are a few within that have never been made available until now.

Self-taught, Noell is known for the unique and minimalist universe she creates and embeds herself in, as both the artist and the subject of her imagery. The photographs in his book depict the hands of prisoners from the early 20th century Turkey, drawn from the photograph albums of Abdul Hamid II, the 34th Sultan of the Ottoman Empire. Hayal & Hakikat(translated as Dream & Fact), by Cemre Yeşil Gönenli, takes the form of two booklets ⁠— A Handbook of Forgiveness and A Handbook of Punishment⁠— which can be viewed side by side.

Abdul Hamid II utilised photography as a tool for documenting the modernisation of the Ottoman Empire at the start of the 20th Century. A photography studio was build inside the Yıldız Palace and albums reproduced and sent across the world as a testament to the progress of the Ottoman Empire. Abdul Hamid II himself rarely left Istanbul but commissioned photographs so he could become acquainted with his own country, otherwise invisible to his eye.

Amongst other things, Abdul Hamid II was obsessed with crime fiction and in the 25th year of his reign he ordered all murder convicts to be photographed with their hands visible, in preparation for a planned amnesty. He has been moved by pseudo-scientific information he had read in a crime novel that “any criminal with a thumb joint longer than the index finger joint, is inclined to murder.” To this end, the photographs in this book show the subjects’ hands for the purpose of classification. They are presented in the book in categories – those chained with iron bracelets and those without. Cemre Yeşil Gönenli, has cropped out the faces of the subjects so their emotional state is ambiguous. The ‘Dream’ of the title refers to the inmates’ desire for release and the “Fact’, their actual circumstances. The fate of the individual prisoners remains unknown as there is no record of the verdict of Abdul Hamid II after viewing the hands awaiting forgiveness.

The book is a result of the workshop ‘Interpreting the Encyclopedia of Istanbul with Photographs’ organised by Geniş Açı Project Office and SALT in May 2019. Cemre Yeşil Gönenli found the story this archive of crime photographs in this unfinished encyclopaedia by Reşat Ekrem Koçu. She then went on to investigate the images preserved in Istanbul University’s Library Collection of Rare Books within the albums of The Yıldız Palace Photography Collection.

Hayal and Hakikat is dedicated to those in contemporary times who are arbitrarily detained.

Cemre Yeşil Gönenli is a photographer, artist and visual story teller, is based Istanbul. She teaches and writes about photography, and runs a small publishing house and photobook shop called FiLBooks in Istanbul.

The images in the book originate from the Istanbul University Library of Rare Books and Special Collections.

On the 100th anniversary of his birth, we pay tribute to Magnumphotographer Erich Hartmann with a selection of his most iconic images.

Erich Hartmann, who would have been 100 years old July 29, 2022 – was a quintessentially 20th-century photographer, both in the story of how he came to be an image maker, and in his pioneering of emerging practices.

Born into a Jewish household in Munich in 1922, little more than a year before Adolf Hitler led the Beer Hall Putsch, he and his immediate family escaped to the US shortly before war broke out in Europe, only to return again five years later as an American soldier. He served in England, France and Belgium before enlisting as a court interpreter at Nazi trials in Cologne, then moved back to the US, settling in New York City. There, he married, had two children, and pursued his interest in photography, studying under Berenice Abbott and Alexey Brodovitch at the New School for Social Research, and later working as a freelancer, making his name with his work for Fortune magazine in the 1950s. He joined Magnum Photos in 1952
